adhd.label: Step 1 · Jumps to Ch. 4: The 1913 Letter That Stunned G. H. Hardy (Start Here)
adhd.brief: Starts at the dramatic turning point in January 1913 when Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy opens a messy envelope from an unknown Madras clerk and realizes these wild infinite series could only come from a genius.

adhd.label: Step 2 · Flashes Back to Prologue & Ch. 1–2: Temple Porch & Carr's Book in Kumbakonam
adhd.brief: Flashes back to South India along the Kaveri River, showing how young Ramanujan worked out thousands of theorems on an elbow-rubbed slate on his porch, experiencing formulas as direct visions from Goddess Namagiri.

adhd.label: Step 3 · Jumps to Ch. 6: Flint and Stone — Pure Intuition Meets Rigorous Proof
adhd.brief: Inside Trinity College, Ramanujan's lightning-fast pattern intuition collides with Hardy's insistence on formal step-by-step proof, producing their breakthrough formula for integer partitions.

adhd.label: Step 4 · Jumps to Ch. 8: Taxicab 1729 & Mock Theta Functions
adhd.brief: Even while ill in Putney and returning to Madras, Ramanujan instantly spots 1729 as the smallest sum of two cubes in two ways and writes down mock theta functions now used in black-hole physics.
